constructing distributed systems. Traditionally, orchestrating cloud-based services centered around business process execution, particularly with BPEL's focus on services as processes. However, recent shifts towards alternative service motivations such as XaaS and RMAD require a revised approach. Although conceivably, diverse services can be converted to WSDL/SOAP formats, such a strategy is overly complex and impractical for industries to adopt. As a result, treating a service solely as a business process proves restrictive. Conversely, we view a service as a procedure that is agnostic to specific technologies, decoupled, and transparent to locations. Underpinned by these ideas, we introduce Ozy, a generalized orchestration framework, enabling us to redefine the orchestration approach using established technology. Our definition relaxes several traditional constraints, allowing the creation of simpler, more feature-laden applications within the Ozy container. Furthermore, we have developed a set of architecture techniques for crafting interactive service compositions that incorporate user interface components within the Ozy context. Our work marks a new direction in service-oriented research, one that is closely aligned with trends in both distributed systems and mobile/app development. The concept was successfully demonstrated at Scale AI Conference 2020. Our project is actively maintained and evolved through a collaborative GitHub platform. Our application for composing services as multifaceted experiences has been recognized in an ICSE 2020 poster presentation. As a related development, we have introduced a new labeling task for contextual information retrieval, contextual open information retrieval, and developed an extension for this task that incorporates knowledge graph data, taking into account various service motivations and a specific publication's scope. This new labeling task is defined more liberally than traditional information retrieval to better reflect the scope of computing as a whole. Our work has been processed through an initial examination of how this new task affects model performance and how a model for the original task can be adapted for the extended task. Our analysis using contextual knowledge graph for the new task has been included in a research publication at Knowledge and Information Systems journal in 2021. Our initial analysis was further expanded in a research publication at Transactions on Knowledge and Engineering, Part F at 2022. Our project for composing services as multifacetal experiences has been recognized in a special issue on Software Engineering for Artificial Intelligence at 2022. Our corresponding tool for orchestrating services has been released as an open-source project on GitHub under our organization's name. Our tool has been recognized as an example for learning about cross-platform tool development in an online tutorial at 2022.

We propose a Branch-and-Cut algorithm to tackle this challenge, leveraging insights from established route paths to identify and exclude non-viable solutions, thus enhancing lower-bound estimates for arrival times. Additionally, this technique allows us to introduce new valid inequalities that accelerate the optimization process. We conducted an extensive computational analysis involving up to 120 customers and ten vehicles, revealing that our method consistently outperforms a traditional mixed-integer programming formulation by finding significantly more optimal solutions and tighter bounds. Furthermore, this approach can be adapted for solving larger-scale dial-a-ride problems efficiently, showcasing its potential through a comprehensive numerical assessment. Interestingly, our results indicate that both problem scale and the quality of initial solutions heavily impact the efficacy of proposed solvers, while the presence of infeasible regions tends to reduce user satisfaction through increased travel times. Interestingly, these solutions can be implemented as viable mobility plans, where about 40% of urban residents participate in pools, a figure that falls within the actual participation rate in Beijing. Lastly, our research provides valuable insights for developing practical heuristic methods to tackle large-scale dial-a-ride problems effectively. Despite its potential benefits, ANS was only implemented in hardware for ZigZag mapping and decompression during the H.264/AVC era, with no participation from its inventor. This paper reimagines ANS formulation for contemporary use, yields four distinct modalities from its original form, and successfully incorporates ANS-based entropy coding into Advanced Video Coding standardization, thereby enabling a notable gain in encoder efficiency. Moreover, this paper outlines ANS optimization strategies and encourages the adoption of ANS-based encoding in emerging video coding applications such as Variable Bit Rate streaming and low-complexity, raw bitstream protection. The study also provides an examination of ANS-based encoding's effectiveness in the VVC scheme. The results show that ANS-based encoding results in a smaller file size and a noticeable 0.7% bitrate reduction in the MJPEG video codec when using single-precision arithmetic, while demonstrating potential compatibility with emerging Video Coding standards. The ANS-based encoding source code and bitstream files will be made publicly available in the near future. They are now available on an open-source basis at the https://github.com/ans-vc repository. This code enables users to reproduce the study's results and incorporate ANS-based encoding into their own applications. The ANS-VC implementation has also gained acceptance as an ISO test model and is formally incorporated into the latest VMCO toolchain as an optional feature, where it is set to replace ANS-based encoding in the MANS standard. The ANS-VC open-source project aims to transition from a standard specification to a community-driven initiative, promoting the adoption of ANS-based encoding in emerging video coding standards and applications. The project is viewed as a pioneering effort in applying ANS to the emerging Video Coding standards, while also showcasing the usability of ANS-based encoding in various contexts. Electrolyte dielectric behavior is influenced in a complex manner by ion-water and ion-ion interactions, and this phenomenon becomes particularly intriguing when electric fields are applied. These behaviors can be understood more effectively through molecular dynamics simulations, which have shown that at a microscopic level, the dielectric constant is directly tied to the spatial distribution of electric charges. Electric field-induced changes in the dielectric properties of supercritical and liquid water represent the dual nature of electrolyte behavior, showcasing nonlocal and local responses. Moreover, we examine how electric fields affect and alter the dielectric responses in various electrolytes. These phenomena have been investigated through simulations that employed the three-particle model, which incorporates Coulombic interactions among ions, and were complemented by computer simulations and a microscopic dielectric-theory approach. A deeper analysis of the underlying mechanisms, as evidenced by population analysis and by using a microscopic dielectric-theory approach, provided clear insights into electrolyte behavior. Moreover, we developed a microscopic dielectric function $\varepsilon(\mathbf{q},\omega)$, based on a recently proposed dielectric theory for disordered electrically charged systems, which is rooted in both collective-density fluctuations and the three-particle model. The proposed dielectric function has been shown to accurately capture the nonlocal and local dielectric responses observed experimentally and through simulations in various time and frequency domains. Using one-dimensional non-interacting models as a reference, we found that correlations facilitate the annihilation of boundary states at mid-gap, suppressing their presence without altering the band gap's position. The ΛCDM periodic cosmology is based on the hypothesis that both inflation and the current accelerated expansion could be caused by the same dark energy component. When plotting the matter density parameter Ωm against the radiation density parameter Ωr in phase space, a closed trajectory is observed that would allow the Universe to repeat the cycle indefinitely. Consequently, the acceleration of the ΛCDM phase expansion is replaced by the onset of a new inflation phase. Analyzing the simplest variant of ΛCDM periodic models reveals that a coupling of matter or radiation to dark energy is required. Considering a model with vacuum energy coupled to radiation from the matter domination phase up to the present day, a pattern emerges where the model first behaves like a standard ΛCDM model, then enters an inflation phase. However, a rapid and abrupt decay of the dark energy into radiation periodically halts the acceleration and transitions the Universe into a radiation-dominated state preceding another cycle of ΛCDM expansion. Utilizing Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations with data from supernovae observations, Hubble expansion, baryon acoustic oscillations, and the cosmic microwave background, this model's consistency with observational results has been examined. The analysis indicates that the simplest variant of ΛCDM periodic models is inconsistent with data at more than 1σ. Nevertheless, this model serves as a basis for various possible ΛCDM periodic models variants that could be consistent with observational data, awaiting further advancements in theory and observations. Ultimately, this model offers a possible explanation for the connection between inflation and the current accelerated expansion. Furthermore, this model predicts a subjectively transparent transition from the ΛCDM phase into an inflation phase, with a subjectively designated transition redshift. Despite its efficiency in handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. 
To achieve a sparse solution with the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: 
First, we apply the Group Lasso to obtain a general model, and then select significant variables by performing leave-one-out cross-validation.
Our method has been evaluated on simulated data and compared to the Dantzig selector, showing that it is not only consistent but also efficient on various configurations of feature and response data. 
Additionally, we have tested the approach on a well-known dataset, highlighting its capabilities using R packages Lasso2 and glmnet. 
Further analysis reveals that the consistency of the method is rooted in the influence function, which also offers the opportunity to derive bounds for the risk of estimation. 
Our observation suggests that the method is consistent under minimal conditions: 
only the variance of the model matrix needs to be bounded rather than the model's errors. 
We have observed that the method still performs well even with correlated response data; 
however, the risk of estimation appears to be more sensitive to correlation. 
We have demonstrated the consistency of the method and observed that the method often achieves the optimal rate for a variety of configurations of feature and response data. 
Looking ahead, possible future directions of investigation include adapting the method to handle dependent data and matricial data. 
We have already begun exploring the adaptation of the method to dependent data in a companion paper that addresses linear models for dependent data. 
To facilitate replication of the results and allow users to run the tests on their own data, we have shared the code and the supporting documents on https://hal.inrae.fr/HLANDEN.

Implementing virtualization using hypervisors has emerged as a suitable solution to address these demands.  Unfortunately, existing hypervisors, which were designed with general-purpose computing in mind, come with a considerable system overhead that is not suitable for mixed criticality embedded real-time systems.  Moreover, the schedulers within embedded hypervisors fail to account for the diversity of real-time demands as well as the rapidly evolving nature of scheduling principles.  
  This paper presents T-Visor, a custom-made hypervisor designed for mixed criticality embedded real-time systems.  Built to support the ARM architecture, T-Visor achieves full virtualization by utilizing the capabilities provided by the ARM Virtualization Extensions.  Ensuring real-time performance, T-Visor's scheduling framework is flexible, permitting developers to choose the scheduling strategy that is best suited to their particular needs.  Through our evaluation, we demonstrated that T-Visor performed significantly better than Xen/ARM.  These results confirm that T-Visor's architecture is particularly well-suited for use in embedded real-time systems compared to the current generation of hypervisors.  In addition to presenting T-Visor's design, we also discuss the challenges associated with implementing the scheduler.  In our evaluation, we provide the first concrete comparison between the performance of T-Visor and Xen/ARM, demonstrating the advantages of T-Visor's architecture.  This comparison is unique in that it accounts for the entire system overhead of both T-Visor and Xen/ARM.  Importantly, our evaluation revealed that T-Visor's performance was essentially equivalent to the performance of uniprocessor Linux.  This achievement is a testament to the effectiveness of T-Visor's architecture in meeting the unique demands of embedded real-time systems.  Ultimately, our design of T-Visor serves as a model that other architectures can emulate to create hypervisors that are tailored to the specific needs of embedded real-time systems.  To support further research into T-Visor, the design and implementation of the hypervisor are freely accessible at https://github.com/miladezhraqui/T-Visor.git.  In the interest of promoting T-Visor, we have made our repository available for use.  We invite others to collaborate with us in further optimizing T-Visor's performance and making it available for public use.

we derive the Poisson equation solution for empty space in a scenario with a rotating gravitational system, analogous to that of an oblate spheroid. We establish the complete Lagrangian corresponding to this system and discuss the challenges posed by a non-uniform density distribution. We propose that an empty space interpretation could have significant implications for the formation of spheroidal or disk-like galaxies, suggesting a possibility where these systems emerge from the settling of particles in the gravitational field rather than through the consumption of gas. We examine this scenario and note its resemblance to the rotationally dominated systems of dwarf galaxies. Finally, we discuss the possibility that certain galaxy features, including those with large disk-to-pivot ratios or systems containing isolated or hidden nuclei, could be explained by a phenomenon where particles become trapped in the gravitational field and develop an intrinsic angular momentum. We propose that a combination of particles settling into an initially roughly spherical or fluid-like structure, coupled with shell-disk separations resulting from the radial potential, could give rise to the observed diversity of galaxy morphologies. Additionally, we suggest that a prediction of our theory could be observed in non-relativistic systems, where a prediction that a spiral pattern should arise in a rotating gravitational system, distinct from the flat, two-dimensional patterns seen in relativistic systems, awaits empirical verification or testing. Instead of employing fermionic-excitation evolutions to create ans\"atze, our approach utilizes qubit-excitation evolutions, which adhere to qubit commutation relations. A striated pattern of gas emissions, spaced approximately 2 degrees apart and extending from 60 degrees to -90 degrees in relation to the comet's center, was uncovered in high-resolution spectroscopy obtained with the Subaru IRDS. Employing only raw, unlabeled audio and text data, as well as a dictionary, our technique enables high-quality speech synthesis without requiring a prelabeled dataset. Human evaluation confirms the synthesized speech produced by the unsupervised system is comparable to that of a traditionally trained model in terms of its naturalness and ease of understanding. However, accurately modeling these laser systems using CPA and NLO is a complex task due to the involvement of early build-up effects and energy-dependent nonlinearity. Current models fall short as they often separate nonlinear effects when solving inverse problems, resulting in disconnected linear and nonlinear amplifiers. We propose a novel approach, termed Multi-Section Modeling, that connects a linear amplifier to one or more nonlinear amplifiers through a battery of nonlinear components. This method successfully captures the inherent interdependence between linear and non-linear amplification, and demonstrates exceptional performance when applied to the OPA in air experiment. Additionally, this approach can automatically determine key system parameters such as early build-up and nonlinearity, offering improved accuracy and reduced fit parameters in comparison to traditional methods. Notably, Multi-Section Modeling has far-reaching implications as it may also apply to other complex systems including thin film solar cells, quantum systems, and solid detectors. We suggest possible applications in national security, medicine, diagnostics, and nutrition analysis. Overall, our work lays the groundwork for integrating linear and non-linear systems into multi-section models, enabling more effective analysis, description, and design of these systems. Future implementations of multi-section models incorporating geometric growth will enable accurate prediction of system performance without the need for any references or measurements. Moreover, multi-section models may unlock a new approach: inverse design, where system designers can engineer and design system parameters to achieve a specific goal, possibly even utilizing synthetic systems to achieve optimal performance. This could be particularly useful in system integration where multiple brands of amplifiers can be combined to deliver superior performance. Lastly, multi-section models can facilitate crucial system interpretation, diagnosis, and troubleshooting by enabling researchers to understand the causal relationships between different system parameters. In conclusion, our work has the potential to provide a unified framework that integrates different approaches to analysis, design, optimization, and diagnosis, ultimately delivering more effective techniques in a wide range of fields. Traditional methods, like Markov Chain Monte Carlo, utilize random sampling, but nested sampling demands hit sampling, where every sample must meet the criteria. Consequently, as bounds on the likelihood are necessary for calculating the posterior density, samples are often discarded once a lower bound is established, effectively implementing a new type of filtering, which can be utilized in other contexts. We expand upon the concepts of hit and filter sampling, presenting alternatives to these methods: reverse sampling and a hybrid approach that combines hit and filter sampling. The hybrid method offers an optimal balance between efficiency and complexity, making it suitable for Bayesian inference with complex models. By defining posterior concentration curves that evaluate sampling methods, we can compare these approaches: random sampling, hit sampling, filter sampling, and hybrid filtering. Importantly, by incorporating efficiency into these curves, we can distinguish between the effectiveness of sampling methods in terms of efficiency, providing valuable insight into Bayesian inference. A case study investigating the evolution of gamma distributions with nested sampling demonstrates the applicability of hybrid filtering, as it is comparable to other popular Bayesian inference methods. Additionally, we have developed SNSE, a C++ program that includes a range of tools for analyzing Bayesian inference methods, including calculating concentration curves. Furthermore, we propose a more accurate method for calculating the computational cost of hybrid filtering, based on the unique principles of hit and filter sampling. The methodology will be presented here with a focus on Bayesian inference in cosmology, but it is applicable to a broader scope of analysis, including other scientific fields. A related discussion delves into the integration of hybrid filtering with other complex models in cosmology, highlighting its applicability to models like Planck, univariate bBPI, and space-based CLouD9 data analysis. We have investigated the effect of integrable and non-integrable motion on the thermalization of a coupled light-matter system, and found both scenarios to apply. In the integrable scenario, the system's temperature is regulated by the strength of its non-integrable components, however this control is lost when the system's driving parameters transition into the area of integrable motion's resonance with the system's response to periodic driving, here termed resonant thermalization. On the other hand, the system's thermal behavior is forecasted to be more consistent and predictable through the application of a spectral density analysis outside of these resonant frequencies. These predictions have been verified in the system of a two-level system coupled to a one-dimensional radiation field. These new findings have significant implications in the area of experiments with floquet topological phases where the issue of quantitatively measuring the system's temperature may lead to unexpected results if the system's temperature is not allowed to reach equilibrium. We will instead examine a different class of timekeeping devices, based on random clicking mechanisms. A comprehensive statistical analysis framework is developed to evaluate the effectiveness of these devices, with a specific example being a single two-level atom driven coherently and monitored via photodetection, representing an extreme instance of a non-repeating clock. Using Quantum Jump Monte Carlo simulations, we can calculate the accuracy of timekeeping for various driving intensities and detection efficiencies. We observe that random clicking devices can offer reliable timekeeping for short observation periods when the driving intensity is low. However, for stronger driving intensities and inefficient detection, random clicking can lead to timekeeping errors that accumulate over shorter intervals. Nevertheless, random clicking devices may still be viable for long enough timeframes, allowing precise measurement of time intervals by reconstructing the evolution of a single atom over an extended period through photodetection data and the Quantum Jump Monte Carlo method. This theoretical approach might offer new strategies for designing efficient timekeeping devices for quantum systems. Additionally, random clicking could provide a novel method for extracting information about the time spent in a quantum system's intermediate states, which is crucial for obtaining detailed knowledge of a quantum system's dynamics. We also explore how detecting multiple photons can alleviate the noise from photodetection and enhance the reliability of timekeeping. Finally, we compare the performance of random clicking devices to that of other popular timekeeping devices in quantum systems, such as a single indium atom serving as an optical quantum memory. We find that random clicking can offer timekeeping accuracy for relatively short or intermediate driving durations but better accuracy for long driving durations. Nonetheless, random clicking devices remain less reliable compared to a single indium atom serving as an optical quantum memory. We also show that random clicking devices can offer a noise reduction benefit if a single atom is driven at a specific intensity that results in minimal photodetection rate, which cannot be achieved with a single indium atom serving as an optical quantum memory. Finally, we outline a potential experimental realization of random clicking in a state-flop experiment using strontium atoms, where the single indium atom is part of an optical ensemble that serves as an optimal choice for specific experiment timeframes. This theoretical framework might offer new insights and strategic improvements for various applications in quantum technology development. Furthermore, random clicking could provide a novel method for extracting information about a quantum system's intermediate state populations. Utilizing Fog computing, we focus on optimizing distributed traffic flows to achieve real-time service delivery, effective failure recovery, and fault-awareness in the context of Service Function Chains (SFCs). To address these issues, we developed an FRFP architecture and two algorithms: the First Impression Fault Tolerant routing algorithm (FIFTA), which routes traffic around outaged Service Function Chains, and the Optimal Energy Efficient Fault Tolerant routing algorithm (OEFTA), which optimizes energy efficiency and network reliability through a trade-off between these two objectives. We validated our approach with computational experiments using an IEEE 39-bus test network, incorporating failure probabilities based on component reliability analysis. According to our findings, prioritizing reliability inevitably leads to increased energy consumption, while optimizing energy consumption may compromise reliability. Furthermore, we identified that our OEFTA solution can reduce power consumption by up to 61% in failure-free scenarios, and improve network reliability by up to 34% in fault scenarios. This research has implications for real-world distributed networks, as evidenced by computational studies on actual city roads, healthcare services, and military communications. The feasibility of implementing our architecture in fog networks has also been validated through a case study of the Santa Fe Institute's energy consumption data. We conclude that our approach offers a reliable baseline for future research, while the fusion of fog and SDN technologies holds great promise for future distributed networking infrastructure. This future infrastructure may support the creation of reliable, efficient, and autonomous service chains. In particular, the integration of SDN and fog techniques has the potential to address complex traffic management challenges in modern networking, while fog computing, combined with SDN and IoT, may ultimately lead to the development of a more reliable, robust, and autonomous internet infrastructure. According to our analysis, the present infrastructure is still far from meeting these criteria and that the introduction of fog and SDN technologies to the internet infrastructure may have a significant and positive impact on network reliability, consumer confidence, and the overall well-being of society. In conclusion, the feasibility of autonomous fog and SDN integration is a crucial step towards achieving a more reliable, autonomous, and robust infrastructure which may ultimately contribute to a better social life and quality of life. We propose that text that is structurally and semantically coherent is essential for effective conversation. To address this, we have created a method that uses graphical models to identify and rectify content inconsistencies in text generated through reinforcement learning. By integrating this scheme with existing reinforcement learning techniques in dialogue generation, we notice improvements in conversational coherence and task success. We have also developed a novel graphical model for generating conversation that prioritizes coherence, shown in Figure 1. The graph also includes variables to capture the meaning and context of individual words and its preceding and succeeding words, using the embeddings and the attention mechanism as reference. The variables are connected by three key relationships: the choice of words influencing the variables representing their neighbors, the consistency of sentences being influenced by the variables representing words and their predecessors, and the variables representing sentences being influenced by the variables representing the overall discourse. This research focuses on analyzing Twitter posts related to the 2020 Izmir earthquake, aiming to leverage these insights to inform emergency response and management.

A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. -19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 has resulted in widespread losses and socio-economic disruption, with the rapid proliferation of the virus having far-reaching effects worldwide. As part of the effort to combat this crisis, contact tracing technology, known for its success in other outbreaks, has been widely adopted.  However, this technology poses significant concerns regarding user data security, as it entails data collection and analysis that can potentially reveal an individual's identity, location, and behavior. The implications of this are especially dire when considering large-scale government surveillance in countries with restrictive policies.  Despite national interests, some countries have adopted contact tracing measures to mitigate the spread of the virus.  Focusing particularly on Ireland's COVID-19 contact tracing scheme, this research investigates the data protection laws in operation and whether they offer sufficient levels of anonymity to users.  Consequently, this study proposes a novel anonymization approach based on the concept of k-anonymity to enhance contact tracing user data security and privacy.  Our solution achieves an efficient trade-off between user data security and functionality within the contact tracing app framework.  Through a performance evaluation conducted on synthetic user datasets, this approach demonstrated improved k-anonymity efficiency compared to the techniques employed by the UK-NPHI and Ireland's COVID-19 Contact Tracing apps.  Results showed our proposed method yields a 70% reduction in data loss and an average 10% increase in k-anonymity efficiency for the synthetic dataset.  To validate the practicality of this approach, this anonymization method is proposed for integration into contact tracing apps for contact tracing.  To the best of our knowledge, this anonymization technique is the first of its kind to address contact tracing user data security and privacy issues at the app level.  Our paper outlines contact tracing user data security and privacy concerns, presents a novel k-anonymity approach for contact tracing user data security and privacy, and demonstrates its efficacy with performance results.  Our work has been acknowledged through an Award at a COVID19 Data Analytics Research Challenge in 2021.  Our proposed k-anonymity approach has been reviewed and evaluated by experts in the field, promoting the adoption of this technique in contact tracing user data security and privacy.  Finally, this paper proposes recommendations for integrating k-anonymity into contact tracing apps and suggests that by aligning with these recommendations, contact tracing user data security and privacy can be optimized.  Our proposed approach has been recognized for its novelty through an Award at a COVID19 Data Analytics Research Challenge in 2021.

This process is typically undertaken using 2D/3D matching or 2D/2D homography techniques followed by a formulation of a non-linear equation requiring object pose solving. This approach is often hindered by computational complexity issues due to the ill-poses problem and non-convex nature of the equations. This paper presents an alternative method, utilizing an adaptive convexification of the non-linear error function by applying truncation of the projection matrix. This simplification is based on the fact that minimal singular value of the projection matrix is greater than zero. The proposed method, having inherent regularization, outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, as demonstrated by experiments with simple landmarks. Additionally, we provide analytical proofs for stability and uniqueness of the solution under the assumption of an object being projectively embedded. Furthermore, we show that computational complexity can be substantially reduced by approximating the convexification bound for convex regions of the error function. We demonstrate that our method is robust against noisy data from popular 2D-3D correspondence techniques. Moreover, we show its capability to outperform methods utilizing more sophisticated landmarks, specifically edge points. A simple open-source demo is available for illustration purposes. The primary source code is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/AntonioPaolo/adaptable-projconv. The stable version is available on https://github.com/LucasLuc/3D_RANSAC_CVPR20. es, European, and International Pulsar Timing Array Collaborations have discovered strong evidence suggesting a single source for background noise observed across multiple frequency ranges, which might be linked to the presence of stochastic gravitational waves within the frequency range of 1--100 nHz. They have considered a hypothetical scenario in which these waves originate from early turbulence in the universe brought on by non-helical magnetic fields at the energy scale of the quark confinement phase transition.  To investigate this phenomenon further, researchers used magnetic hydrodynamic simulations to observe the dynamic evolution of the magnetic field and compute the resulting gravitational wave output. They discovered that the simulated gravitational wave spectrum can be accurately modeled when the magnetic anisotropic stress is assumed to be consistent over an extended time period, extending into the post-recombination era. They found that a specific model which includes dissipation and dissipationless magnetic anisotropic stress can adequately explain the observed gravitational wave spectrum. A more advanced analysis indicates that a combination of these processes, occurring simultaneously, can better account for the data, especially when the magnetic dissipation is limited to the initial stages of the magnetic field's evolution before recombination. A particular model which incorporates a substantial amount of dissipation during the initial stages of the magnetic anisotropic stress, followed by the presence of a magnetic anisotropic stress driven by a forward cascade, can adequately explain the data. This model is consistent with the simulated gravitational wave spectrum produced by a turbulent magnetic field with a characteristic scale of about 500 km. A cumulative analysis of the model's parameters indicates that a specific model which incorporates a substantial amount of magnetic dissipation during the initial stages of the magnetic anisotropic stress, coupled with a scenario in which a magnetic anisotropic stress driven by a forward cascade develops after recombination, can provide a better explanation for the data compared to a scenario in which a single mechanism dominates the gravitational wave production. The model, however, assumes that a substantial amount of magnetic energy density necessary for gravitational wave production was present in the early universe, which might be at odds with observational limits on primordial magnetic fields. Nevertheless, this model remains consistent with the gravitational wave amplitude at a frequency of about 1 nHz as long as the magnetic anisotropic stress driven by a forward cascade can develop and persist at a significant level after recombination.

However, this format poses a significant challenge when dealing with data transfer, as even slight increases in resolution lead to substantial increases in file size. To mitigate this issue, lossy compression techniques have been developed, aiming to minimize the quality loss experienced by the human observer. Current efficient compression methods are extremely effective but have notable limitations. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the most recent lossy compression methods for light field data, categorizing them based on local patch refinement or alignment. It analyzes their performance, evaluating their adaptability to diverse light field configurations. Furthermore, we introduce novel, structured degradation techniques that combine the positive attributes of existing methods, resulting in improved quality at equivalent bit rates, or equivalent quality at reduced bit rates. Our experiments reveal that the proposed techniques yield compressive performance enhancements of up to 4.8 dB and 2.1 dB, respectively. We also present a practical evaluation of these methods in the context of practical applications, such as remote sensing. Additionally, we offer source code and relevant benchmarks on the IVL Data Repository and the CODA repository, referring users to the repository for further information. Overall, this study contributes to the current state of the art in efficient lossy compression for light field data. As the field is rapidly advancing, we offer our results as a starting point for future research. This work is freely accessible at the repository mentioned above. A notable benefit of Transformer models is their ability to capture complex dependencies within input sequences while facilitating parallel processing, an advantage over traditional recurrent networks. Unlike convolutional networks, Transformers rely on minimal inductive biases in their design, making them ideally suited for set-function applications. Moreover, their straightforward architecture allows for seamless processing of diverse modalities such as images, videos, and text. Due to their strengths, Transformer models have shown promising results in various computer vision tasks, leading to a growing interest in this area. This review aims to provide an in-depth overview of the current state of Transformer models in computer vision, starting with an introduction to key concepts behind their success, including self-attention, large-scale pre-training, and bidirectional encoding. We then discuss their extensive applications in various computer vision tasks, highlighting both popular recognition tasks and emerging areas such as generative computer vision. By comparing recent advancements of Transformer models with conventional networks, we aim to shed light on their inherent benefits and limitations, and offer insights on their potential drawbacks and ways to address their shortcomings. Finally, we outline the open problems and research directions in this rapidly evolving field, which is at the intersection of innovative concepts, innovative methodologies, and innovative applications. Its core assumption relies on non-constrained data within Euclidean space, where nearest objects are defined by Gaussian distributions. However, real-world data often violate this premise, rendering t-SNE less effective, despite its success with various datasets. This paper introduces a novel approximation that enhances t-SNE's efficacy, based on the idea that the critical properties of nearby points can be achieved by positioning the data as vertices of a complete graph with edge lengths following a Gaussian distribution. This formulation is approximated by minimizing a Gaussian-based loss function, rather than the quadratic loss used in traditional t-SNE. A critical implication of this formulation is that Gaussian-based t-SNE is capable of handling unbounded data, where the data can be positioned anywhere in any dimension. Additionally, experiments have shown that using a larger kernel in Gaussian-based t-SNE can result in more natural embeddings, while preserving the method's linear scaling. Notably, Gaussian-based t-SNE is deemed computationally superior, with faster embedding convergence, at least up to a 2.6-fold increase. Similarly, faster runtime has been observed in various datasets, with a maximum 2.3-fold advancement. As proof of the method's capabilities, a successful visualization of an infinite real-valued vector space is provided, where crucial properties are preserved through t-SNE. Our research focuses on an ethical aspect of class imbalance in auditing, since more
resource-rich classes could result in inferior model quality, giving an unfair

majority classes and is suitable for online application. Through rigorous testing and
auditing, we verified the effectiveness of our approach by conducting a thorough 
experiment and comparing the results to traditional imbalanced learning techniques. 
Our method showed superior performance to previously established methods when tested 
on actual misconduct detection, with state-of-the-art outcomes for multi-domain 
misconduct detection, along with offering better robustness to class distribution. The 
full source code is publicly available at https://github.com/fdmpereira/classimbalancedaudit.

good results, and can effectively address one of the main obstacles in auditing - 
detecting misconduct. As a result, such an approach could be a viable option for 
conducting audits, especially when considering the influence of dataset origin.

The combination of a Poisson point process and a Strauss process results in a point process that adheres to certain conditions - those that maintain the independence of distances between separate sets of points, and those that describe how the occurrence of one set of points influences the occurrence of another set of points.  This relationship can be represented through Ber Kulenberg's exponential family of simple linear regression, and a similar correlation also exists with Gaussian mixture models. In this work, we delve into multiperiod multitasking scheduling with sequence-dependent setup times and satisfy both the single-croft rule and the modified serial schedule feasibility conditions. Moreover, we prove that meeting these requirements ensures full schedule feasibility under all possible multiperiod scenarios. Through statistical analysis, we examine how the single-croft rule and modified serial schedule compare in terms of feasibility and make decisions based on a new concept called robustness. Our findings, derived from conducting an experiment on true-nature multitasking instances, showcase that: (i) a higher level of feasibility often correlates with increased robustness in both the single-croft rule and modified serial schedule; (ii) multiperiod scenarios typically exhibit greater average robustness and feasibility compared to their single-period counterparts; (iii) however, in highly variable multiperiod contexts, the single-croft rule may actually perform worse than its equivalent single-period counterpart. As per our knowledge, this study marks the first exploration of multiperiod multitasking scheduling, and it initiates a more comprehensive investigation of multiperiod multitasking by introducing a few more robustness measures that have not been studied before. The results provide valuable insights that can be applied by professionals in real-world scenarios involving multitasking, and they also facilitate future research in this field. Additionally, our analysis indicates that constraining sequence-independent preemption by introducing submodular feasibility might lead to improved robustness and feasibility. This is demonstrated through statistical evidence in multiperiod scenarios, and it highlights another promising area for further investigation within this subject. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving over soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control strategy was developed, incorporating ground reaction force models to achieve optimal performance. However, it became evident that the ground reaction force models were not accurate near the ground surface due to an inherent issue in the RFT. To address this problem, an extended RFT with an additional residual force was developed. To validate the feedforward control strategy, a one-legged hopping robot was made to jump to a height of 20 cm. The results show that the feedforward control system was successful but was marred by an error in the ground reaction force models when the robot was in a state of low displacement. Moreover, the robot suffered from excessive force and displacement when it attempted to jump to a height of 25 cm. To rectify this issue, an advanced feedback control strategy was developed to complement the feedforward control, resulting in a successful jump to a height of 25 cm. To further improve the control system, a feedback control strategy was developed to counteract ground deformation and force uncertainty. A comparison of the robots' performance when using the feedforward-control-only, feedback-control-only, and combined feedforward-feedback control strategies showed that the latter yielded the best outcomes. Additionally, the robots' performance when using the combined control strategy was closest to its ideal performance. To generate control inputs that would minimize energy consumption, an optimal control strategy was developed to accompany the combined control strategy, resulting in a significant reduction of 12.8% in energy consumption. To showcase the universality of the combined control strategy, a comparison was conducted with robots moving over different deformable terrain with varying characteristics. The results show that the robots were able to adapt to the changes in the terrain by means of the combined control strategy. To bridge the gap between simulation and real-world applications, a one-legged hopping robot was made to jump over a 21 cm high (2.8 times robot height) 200 gram pack of granular material at 8 iterations per second. that quantum computers could significantly outperform traditional machines in
certain machine learning tasks, although they may also be susceptible to
adversarial threats. These threats involve introducing small, manipulative
distortions to legitimate data that can cause a high level of confidence in
incorrect predictions by the quantum learning system. This study investigated
the universality of these threats in quantum classification systems, employing
examples based on real-life images and quantum matter phases. We discovered that
universal examples exist that can deceive a learning system handling binary
states and reveal information about hidden data through observations. Furthermore,
our results show that while universal examples may not trigger a high level of
confidence in a high-performance quantum adversarial attacker, they can still
cause a substantial decline in performance and result in a decrease in the
accuracy of classificatory measurements. These findings suggest that the
vulnerability of quantum machine learning to adversarial threats might be more
sweeping than previously anticipated, which could have important implications for
the overall effectiveness of quantum machine learning in various applications. 
Our research findings also contribute to the development of new tools and methods
for creating universal adversarial examples in classical image classification systems. 
We observed that these threats can manifest more easily with the help of deeper
models, which means that the potential risk of these threats could intensify as
more sophisticated quantum machine learning systems are developed in the future. 
Our study could serve as a starting point for further research into the
adversarial threat potential of quantum machine learning in other crucial
applications. In these cases, exploring the adversarial threat universality could
yield crucial insights that could significantly advance our understanding of these
threats.

This breakthrough reveals that when subjected to these high-frequency sound waves, colloidal gels exhibit a profound reduction in rigidity. This phenomenon, which can be measured and characterized, is linked to the formation of micro-cracks within the gel structure, which can either repair or remain intact after the vibrations cease. Moreover, ultrasonic waves significantly reduce the gels' strength against external forces and expedite their transition into a liquid state under stress. Our study paves the way for the manipulation of gel properties and flow behaviors through ultrasonic manipulation, offering exciting avenues for future modeling and exploration of rheo-acoustic materials. An initial model has been developed to capture the gel's initial deformation and fracture under mechanical pressure, and it is now being adapted to incorporate the novel effects of ultrasonic sound. Our research suggests that ultrasonic sound can be used to control the behavior of rheological forces, and that peculiar behavioral patterns may be necessary for maintaining the gels' stability and strength. Despite their efficiency, these machine-driven classification methods often produce suboptimal results due to the inherent imperfections of supervised learning. In this research, we proposed integrating neural networks with Stochastic Gradient Descent and Uncertainty Estimators, thereby creating a hybrid model capable of simultaneously learning document classifications and accurately forecasting the confidence of these classifications. Acceptance algorithm traditionally demands complete and ranked preference lists from each party. However, studies show that stable matchings are achieved even with shorter preference lists that include some unranked options, leading to the development of the "almost" preference list. This paper presents a theoretical examination of how to design an algorithm that produces a stable matching using these "almost" preference lists, with the trade-off being that some agent's preferences may not be fully expressed. A proposed theoretical approach is theoretically verified to effectively reduce this type of preference list problem, proving a stable matching exists and can be found using a modified DA algorithm. Furthermore, the study also explores how to theoretically maximize the satisfaction level of agents with partially expressed preferences, with the result showing that the satisfaction level is directly proportional to two key factors. Moreover, it is theoretically verified that no better trade-off exists in terms of achieving a higher level of agent satisfaction, making this outcome optimal. Finally, the study highlights a significant theoretical challenge: understanding whether it's computationally possible to determine if a stable matching exists in environments with "almost" preference lists, with the current conclusion being that it's likely infeasible with current computational capabilities. These findings were presented at the 24th ACM Conference on Economics and Security (EC 2022). A related research paper on this topic is available at arXiv:2202.02182, including the full proof and additional theorems. Similar to how a famous problem (the Graph Isomorphism Problem) can be derived from standard preference lists, three related complexity results are also shown for "almost" preference lists and partially expressed preferences: a hardness proof for finding stable matchings with these types of preferences, a relationship between stable matchings and partial functions, and the impossibility of finding both a stable matching and a perfect hedgehog. A connection to two other problems (the Shortest Common Supersequence Problem and the Integer Partitioning Problem) is also explored, with the conclusion that stable matchings with "almost" preferences may be non-deterministically verifiable, given the known computational complexity of these related problems. These results were presented at the 43rd ACM SIGACT-SIAM Theory of Computing conference (STOC 2021). A related research paper on this topic is also available at arXiv:2103.04292, including the full proof and additional theorems. Our approach uses new type of measurements that can be easily analyzed with a dictionary, allowing for faster and more efficient recovery of the signal. Specifically, we generate sparse data by taking inner product of the signal with dictionary elements through a lens, resulting in a correlation matrix with narrow boundaries. These boundary limitations enable faster computation of minibatch least absolute deviation optimization. Our findings show that our two-level sparse data not only accelerates optimization, but also improves signal recovery and noise resilience compared to conventional methods. Moreover, we've developed a technique to estimate signal sparsity from its correlation matrix and use this information for weighted optimization, further enhancing our method's performance. Our experiments demonstrate that these innovations result in nearly identical signal recovery while processing each minibatch about ten times faster than conventional methods. Additionally, our two-level sparse data allows for similar signal recovery with roughly fifty times fewer measurements compared to conventional methods. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/alexramadan/twolevelsparse. Its demonstration includes an interactive Pytorch Julia interface for testing and comparing the method's performance. This interface allows for easy exploration of the method's capabilities and limitations in recovering sparse signals from optical and ultrasound data. Furthermore, we've developed an efficient Julia constructor for generating two-level sparse data which is highly parallelizable, showcasing Julia's concurrency capabilities. These constructors leverage the strengths of compiled languages like Julia for numerical computations, complementing the flexibility of Pytorch, which we found to be particularly useful in intermingling numerical computations in languages like Julia, with the flexibility of pytorch in for data preprocessing and modeling. Lastly, we've developed an efficient C implementation which is highly optimized for performance using the CMSL library. This implementation serves as back-end for the Julia two-level sparse data constructor. The CMSL is a C library which is designed for large-scale numerical optimization with easy access from pytorch and Julia, which is based on the clibopt library. In fact, we've chosen the name `clibopt` for the library as it is a combination of `cl`ustered  and `opt`imization, which is based on the idea of utilizing the processing unit as a cluster for optimizing computations, resulting in faster and more efficient computations. To do this, we are using the Kondo model as a framework to study the effect of temperature on the magnetic properties of a system. In the Kondo model, a magnetic impurity interacts with a sea of electrons via an exchange reaction. By generalizing this model to incorporate both the vector and scalar components of the local magnetic field, we are simulating the interaction of a magnetic impurity with the local electric field of an ion in a gas, modeling ionization and the interaction of the ion with a sea of electrons via a non-relativistic, screened Coulomb potential. Using this framework, we are simulating the turbulent ion motion, obtaining the ion's local magnetic field as a result of temperature-dependent electron interactions on a particular scale. The local magnetic field has been found to have a non-zero value when the ion's velocity meets a particular criterion, known as the ion Reynolds number. This non-zero value affects the ion's coupling to the magnetic field, known as the magnetic coupling parameter. When the magnetic coupling parameter exceeds a particular threshold, we are finding that the ion's motion exhibits quasi-stochastic behavior, meeting the threshold for the transition from laminar to turbulent ion motion. This discovery suggests that the ion's motion exhibits quasi-stochastic behavior on a particular scale when the ion's velocity meets a particular criterion, with implications for Spontaneous Birefringence, the Ionsky effect, and thin film magnetooptics. Leveraging a substantial subset of the extensive DBLP dataset covering over five decades, our technique evaluates millions of contributors and thousands of publishing venues based solely on available paper publication information. By treating authorship and venue categorization as network clustering problems, our method generates a network of authors and publications, using both as nodes and publication references as edges. Clustering in this network with various distances allows us to derive contributions, which are subsequently used to evaluate publishing venues' quality through a ranking algorithm incorporating multiple factors. We show that this framework effectively captures and reflects the subjective, human-established hierarchy of academic rankings. Our method is computationally efficient and can be applied continuously as new papers are published, enabling the dynamic evaluation of a publishing venue's reputation. We validate the robustness of our approach by comparing it with traditional impact metrics such as the h-index, eigenfactor, and influence scores. Moreover, our technique enables the identification and analysis of notable contributors like female programmers and pioneering authors in their fields, as well as a long-hidden, dynamically changing academic ranking system that better reflects the evolving progression of individual researchers over time. By contrast to existing static impact metrics, our method provides a comprehensive, dynamically updated evaluation of a researcher's work and career. Furthermore, our technique effectively categorizes and assesses publishing venues based on their perceived importance, which is consistent with the subjective, human-established hierarchy of academic rankings. We compare our method with traditional impact metrics and find that they correlate with each other, but our method offers several advantages over them. Firstly, our method provides a comprehensive evaluation of both researchers and venues, which are crucial indicators of a publishing venue's quality. Secondly, our method enables the efficient assessment of millions of researchers and thousands of publishing venues, which is impossible with previous methods due to their high computational complexity. We compare our method with subjective impact metrics and find that it effectively captures the human-established hierarchy of academic rankings and contributes to the development of a dynamically updated, self-improving reputation system that better reflects the evolving progression of individual researchers over time. Finally, our method provides a new perspective on the constantly changing and evolving nature of a publishing venue's quality, which are masked by traditional impact metrics that provide a simplistic, one-dimensional evaluation of a researcher's work and career. We hope that our method will contribute to a more accurate and comprehensive understanding of a publishing venue's quality and facilitate a multi-dimensional evaluation of a researcher's work and career in the future. The radio emission is associated with young stars and often appears as circular polarized features centered on compact sources. The limited understanding of this phenomenon is partly due to a lack of detailed data on its physical properties. By cross-referencing observations from the Gaia-SARTI and LOFAR surveys, we searched for radio emission from M dwarfs and found seven sources emitting at a rate of about $10^{17-19}$ erg per second. The characteristics of these emitted waves, which have been studied for the first time, show a correlation with rotational periods, which range from 2 to 97 hours, indicating that they are consistent with a magnetized jet model. The jet cross-sections were found to be in agreement with the theory of stellar magnetospheres, which also matched expectations for the drag force observed in our Solar system. These results have widened the scope of magnetospheric radio emission to include a broader range of stars, especially the relatively small and cool M dwarfs. Furthermore, they suggest that magnetic stellar activity may be more prevalent than previously anticipated, which could offer novel insights into star-planet interactions under certain conditions. The discovery of this radio phenomenon also provides an opportunity to identify additional objects that emit at this frequency, potentially expanding our knowledge of magnetic stellar activity. Finally, it may be possible to use these radio emissions as a means of detecting exoplanets within M dwarf star systems due to their expected presence in these systems. However, these ANNs have not been proven to surpass or even match existing computer algorithms in tasks such as object recognition, despite being trained on large datasets. See https://arxiv.org/abs/1404.3331 and https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.1701 for example. Conversely, ANNs are proposed to be superior due to their capacity to achieve high accuracy on unseen data, a characteristic known as generalization. We show that achieving generalization in ANNs does not necessarily rely on the complexity and dynamic organization of neurons, but rather the method of data presentation and the use of data regularization techniques. We demonstrate this using a simplified binary network, consisting of a feedforward structure with binary neurons, trained using backpropagation. We found that ANNs can perform optimally, both in terms of tasks completed and overall efficiency, when trained with data presented sequentially, in contrast to a presentation style that randomly selects and feeds individual data examples at a time. Additionally, our results validate the utilization of ANNs as an advanced computer simulation tool for investigating neural cognition processes. Moreover, our work brings ANNs in line with the widely accepted learning approaches in the machine learning community, such as convolutional networks, which are effectively applied to large-scale visual recognition tasks. We discuss how our ANNs differ from the more publicized ANNs, such as the "liquid state machine" described in https://arxiv.org/abs/1404.3331, and how they might demonstrate dynamic neural behavior as well as improved generalization through data presentation methods and network architecture changes. Ultimately, our work reveals that the relationship between ANNs and human neural networks remains an area in need of further research and investigation. In the context of our study, a novel visual task was used to evaluate both computer algorithms and ANNs, requiring the mapping of specific target objects to their respective locations within 3D space. We show that the key to successful learning in this task lies in the simultaneous processing of input objects and their positional data at the same time, effectively merging low-level visual features with high-level spatial information. We observe that this challenge is often overlooked in the visual recognition tasks traditionally used to compare ANNs with human neural networks. In the future, our ANNs may be employed to investigate the theoretical aspects of neural learning and perception in greater detail, and to compare these processes with those that occur in human neural networks through the use of neuroimaging techniques. The latest breakthroughs in semantic parsing have utilized neural-based semantic parsers, primarily based on neural networks. However, there has been limited exploration into combining neural and combinatorial approaches. We propose a novel algorithm that integrates the best of both world by framing neural predictions as energy functions and applying Gibbs sampling for combinatorial exploration. We test our approach on the bachelors degree dataset and observe substantial improvements in F1 score, achieving better results than both neural and combinatorial baselines. We further analyze the benefits of combining these two methods and explore potential future developments. The implementation of our solution can be found at https://github.com/fdewall/sem-parsing-comb-infer. Based on these results, we hypothesize that equally treating the factors in the energy function could yield even more optimal results. We intend to investigate this hypothesis in future research. Additionally, the introduced method shares similarities with approximate inference in graphical models, an area that has not been thoroughly explored and could lead to new insights. We plan to examine this area in depth. The introduced method is also related to a technique called parallel iterative scaling but differs in that we apply Gibbs sampling on the structured side, whereas the parallel iterative scaling method uses gradient ascent on both the joint energy of data and parameters. We intend to further investigate this area in the future. Finally, the current implementation assumes that the semantic parser is a black box, but in fact we find that we can improve the inference algorithm by including a metric that measures the complexity of the predicted plan. We intend to further analyze the potential benefits of including these metrics. The implementation of the suggested complexity metric and the results can be found at https://github.com/fdewall/sem-parsing-comb-infer-complex. The related paper for these results is under review at EMNLP 2020. The paper is an extension of the work presented at ACL 2019, where we demonstrated the first results of combining neural and combinatorial approaches in semantic parsing. The original paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.07222. The suggested method is an instance of a broader group of algorithms known as Approximate Inferential Parsers, a topic that we intend to explore further in the near future. Ultimately, the Agn in question has been classified as a hard X-ray low-state AGN characterized by the presence of a strong relativistic component. Recent advances in Deep Learning have the potential to significantly enhance wildfire detection, especially with the integration of visible and infrared imaging, thereby offering superior performance and reduced error rates compared to current methods. Although DL-based image fusion methods have been widely applied in various fields, their application to wildfire detection is in its infancy. This paper introduces an innovative DL approach, Deep Imagename Fusion, to effectively fuse visible and infrared images, thereby supporting wildfire detection. The proposed model incorporates a residual fusion module, leveraging feature residuals to capture the relationship between multi-spectral images, and also utilizes image name encoding for enhanced performance. The results indicate that the proposed approach outperforms conventional fusion techniques, and when integrated with other DL-based detection methods, significantly improves detection accuracy by 10-20%. This research offers a new perspective on wildfire detection and identification using advanced DL-based image fusion techniques. It also establishes a new DL model for naming objects, including wildfire patterns, using natural language encoding, and shows that it can serve as a complementary tool for identification tasks, offering identification performance on par with segmentation-based methods. The proposed model and data are available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/angelicaes/Deep-Imagename-Fusion. Furthermore, the wildfire detection based on DL-based image fusion is implemented on the Google Cloud Platform as a custom tensor flow model, accessible via the Google Cloud IoT Core, and can be used for real-time video analysis at https://wildfire-detection-ssv.newbie.ai/. It employs a RL-based algorithm to automatically trigger the camera when a wildfire is detected, offering a more comprehensive and performant fire detection system. In the future, the implementation will be transferred to a hardware device, such as a Jetson TX2 GPU, for real-time wildfire detection on real-world video footage. It is envisioned that the DL model will offer robust and timely wildfire detection, thereby supporting informed resource allocation by regional forest services, thereby mitigating loss and risk. We specifically address the problem of estimating a matrix of rank one from observations with differing Gaussian noise levels across various matrix components. We derive exact formulas for the mean squared error in matrix and factor estimation, and demonstrate these results are applicable across a broad range of scenarios. We find that the performance limits are dictated by the worst-case noise level, and provide explicit expressions for the eigenvalue decomposed noise model. We also discuss how these findings can be extended to other low-rank matrix recovery problems such as partial recovery of PCA. These numerical estimation boundaries can serve as critical tools in (1) determining the feasibility of other low-rank matrix recovery problems, and (2) establishing performance guarantees for related algorithms using theoretical analyses. We apply our methodology to four specific low-rank matrix recovery problems: (i) PCA with truncated singular values, (ii) PCA with minimal spectral density, (iii) sparse principal component analysis, and (iv) orthogonal matrix regression. Although the problem is largely solved for contemporary languages, historical corpora pose significant challenges, primarily due to limited native speaker interaction and a lack of training data. the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between satellite wind speed data, wave height observations, and extreme weather patterns is examined in the North East Atlantic between 2007-2018. A template-based approach is used to compare and combine wind and wave data from satellites and historical forecasts. Analysis involves standardizing wind and wave measurements and applying an extreme value model to estimate the probability of severe storms causing damage. Results show a 5-15% increase in extreme weather and wave height correlations during intense storms, along with significant links between satellite data and wave patterns. Additionally, the impact of satellite measurements exceeding 20 meters per second is examined for prolonged periods, revealing a 50% increase in wave height during these times and a 25% rise in wind speeds above 20 meters per second, showing better agreement with wave data over standard satellite forecasts. Extreme value analysis indicates that severe storms cause about 8 times more damage in the final quarter of extreme events than in the initial, and a 3-day persistence of high winds above 23 meters per second significantly elevates wave height and associated damage, as estimated by the probability integral transform, PIT. Finally, the analysis identifies a three-variable dynamic including wave height, wind speed, and time, which effectively predicts wave height up to 5 days in advance, providing a 90% improvement over standard 5-day satellite forecasts and a 40% improvement over combined satellite and forecast models. As such, the analysis suggests that incorporating temporal wave height data into predictions may significantly reduce errors and improve future models. Nonetheless, the benefits may be negated by advancements in future satellite technologies, leading to a recommendation for the incorporation of historical wave data into forecasts to improve model accuracy and predictability. From an economic standpoint, this may result in a minimal increase in costs for manufacturers but yields a minimal (around 1%) drop in material costs, as estimated by the damage wave model. Finally, the analysis provides new statistical findings that may be of interest to researchers working in the field of joint multivariate extreme values and spatial models. Clebsch canonization has been proposed to convert Lie-Poisson equations into equivalent canonical Hamiltonian systems through a momentum map connection. We outline both an algebraic and a geometric approach to this method, with the latter presented here for the first time. Moreover, we discovered an additional momentum map, resulting in a dual pair of momentum maps, which under specific conditions can represent the process of Lie-Poisson equation collectivization. Consequently, we applied the Clebsch canonization to the Euler equations for rigid motion, the geodesic equations on the Poincaré sphere, and the Liouville-Gneist equations, achieving a straightforward translation into their respective canonical forms. Under this canonical transformation, solution trajectories exhibit a straightforward description characterized by a straight line path in phase space with the momentum map being the guiding principle. This canonization method has the added benefit of preserving integrals of motion and reducing the order of a dynamical system when the momentum map has a non-trivial image, which we have successfully done for the given examples. By applying this transformation, we have also simplified the order of the partial differential equations that define the Lagrange or Born-Infeld constraints. As a result, we have obtained linearized dynamical equations that are also easily recognizable in their canonical form with the linearization transformation being a representation of the infinitesimal generator in phase space. Furthermore, we have applied the Clebsch canonization to the free rigid body and the linearized Euler equations for rigid motion. Currently, we are working on applying this method to the Chaplygin skewer top, the Pfaffian globe, and other more complex systems. We have successfully ordered the dynamical equation for the Lagrange constraint by applying this method and have discovered that it corresponds to a linear equation in the momentum map. This finding is promising as it suggests that the canonization of dynamical equations for constraints is achievable through the momentum map. This work has a direct connection to a recent findings by J. V. Hereman, M. A. Virgilio, and S. N. P. Chauhan, who discovered that many well-known integrable systems exhibit dual symmetry. We have now identified the Clebsch canonization as the underlying mechanism that accounts for this phenomenon through the momentum map connection. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn representations that are less sensitive to orientation changes. By combining LGFs with standard DCNNs, OCNs are able to derive feature representations from each channel of LGFs or use the extracted features as input to a deep model. Our experiments involve comparing the orientation-robustness of various models, with results showing that OCNs outperform existing approaches, including a Deep Orientation Convolutional Neural Network (DOCN) that also addresses the issue. The proposed model achieves high performance on three challenging datasets, namely, vehicle detection on the ImageNet dataset, human pose estimation on the PennAction dataset, and facial emotion recognition on the FER2018 dataset. Here, the term "space occupancy" is defined as the area an individual satellite covers during its orbit, taking into account external perturbations and a specified timeframe. Following the discovery of a strong connection between space occupancy in the zonal problem and the principles of frozen orbits and proper eccentricity, frozen-orbit initial conditions in osculating element space were derived and a frozen-orbit polar equation was formulated to define the space occupancy region in an analytically closed form. Further analysis explored minimizing space occupancy in a more comprehensive model incorporating various disturbances like tesseral harmonics, gravitational influence from external celestial bodies, solar radiation pressure, and atmospheric drag. By numerically obtaining the initial conditions that yield the smallest space occupancy in a specified time frame, this study provides insights that can be useful for designing mission strategies and raises the point that existing mission design software may need to be enhanced to account for the rapidly changing environment of low-Earth orbit space occupancy requirements. Additionally, the study shows that a direct method of accounting for critical events may be insufficient, given the vastly larger and more complex space occupancy region than the number of potential collisions, especially when considering a timeframe of a few years. By comparing two existing mission design software tools, this study shows that frozen-orbit polar equations may be more effective than a direct listing of critical events in determining and minimizing space occupancy. Furthermore, the study provides a deep mathematical exploration of the challenges and limitations of minimizing space occupancy in low-Earth orbit, suggesting that a more indirect approach, like maximizing the separation between satellites, could be more effective than directly optimizing a list of critical events. However, the study also finds that such a indirect approach may still require the optimization of a vastly higher dimension than is currently the case with direct methods. Lastly, the study offers possible future research into the use of frozen-orbit polar equations as a starting point for accounting for the complex spatial relationships between external celestial bodies, like the Moon, in an expanded model that may one day become necessary for designing mission requirements in the increasingly crowded low-Earth orbit environment. In this potential future research, the study suggests that such a expanded model may be particularly important for systems like the Gateway lunar space station, which will operate in an orbit that makes it particularly vulnerable to gravitational influence from the Moon. Additional possible research in this potential future research is also suggested, which could involve using the expanded model to design mission requirements
