This resulted in significant reductions in computation for each iteration, reaching an O(N logN) complexity. Nevertheless, the kernel's conditioning number still dominated the overall computational time. This paper tackles this issue by introducing a preconditioner specifically designed for kernelized Sinkhorn matrices. By applying this preconditioner, we eliminate the linear term resulting from the kernel's conditioning, leaving only a lower-order term. We provide theoretical justification for our approach and demonstrate that it can be implemented efficiently, resulting in a reduced overall computational time. We combine this preconditioner with the accelerated kernel-based Sinkhorn iteration, yielding a truly linear solver. This means that the computational time should increase only linearly with respect to the matrix's size and not quadratically. We support our claim with empirical evidence showcasing the benefits of our approach. To accommodate various kernel types, such as Gaussian and Laplacian kernels, we introduce an anisotropic scaling of Sinkhorn iterations. This technique can be used independently to further accelerate the solver, especially when dealing with kernels that have ill-conditioned kernel matrices. We apply this scaling to achieve improved results. We provide empirical evidence that our solver is orders of magnitude faster than classical solutions for various minimization problems, even outperforming state-of-the-art algorithms like MatchNet. We demonstrate that our approach can also improve the accuracy of unsupervised OT-based learning methods by leveraging the solver's capabilities to compute larger and more precise OT plans, which were not possible due to the limitations of previous solvers. Intuitively, computing OT plans becomes a bottleneck in optimizing OT-based learning objectives, causing a constraint where the feasibility of an OT plan is directly linked to the solution's optimality. We introduce a new criterion for declaring optimality based on the solver's accuracy, allowing us to stop Sinkhorn iteration when the solver converges to a sufficient precision. This method can run the solver indefinitely or stop it at any time, leveraging the computed OT plan as an approximation. We study and compare the behavior of this criterion in OT-based learning, yielding substantial improvements in training time and, in some cases, improved accuracy. A newly developed robotic scanning technique combines deep learning with user-controlled input, allowing a novice operator to accurately identify the main trunk and posterior curves of the spine. This method pairs a deep neural network with a handheld ultrasound probe, guided by the operator's hand movements, which corrects the focal position as needed. In a small study, 10 fresh cadaveric spines were scanned using the robotic technique, and the results showed that posterior emphyse and liver locations were within 10 mm of their actual positions, while the anterior femoral shaft alignment was within 5 mm. This method is being considered for use in clinical settings, including both local and remote diagnoses. Based on the study's findings, a single user could learn and master the robotic scanning technique within 15-30 minutes, producing reliable and reproducible outcomes. The accuracy of this approach is on par with that of experienced scoliosis researchers, who relied on ultrasound-only assessments. A notable advantage of this method is its potential for remote dignostics, as it does not require the presence of an additional person, aside from the operator. In the future, the usability of this technology will be further investigated for both healthy individuals and patients with scoliosis, with potential applications extending beyond ultrasound to other imaging modalities. Ultimately, this method could reduce costs, expand accessibility to under-resourced areas, and facilitate the development of automated scoliosis detection software. By combining deep learning with user-controlled input, the robotic scanning technique is both innovative and intuitive, which could pave the way for future advancements in ultrasound diagnosis. It is suggested that the perceived focal point of the ultrasound probe serves as a reliable control mechanism for training scoliosis-specific deep learning models. The study further examines potential applications of inferring focal points in other clinical settings, such as breast and liver cancer detection. A conceivable extension of this idea is the creation of an end-to-end diagnostic model incorporating both the neural network and scoliosis-specific focal point estimator. A combination of these components could yield high-precision diagnostic outcomes, matching those of prior ultrasound assessments in the presence of an experienced surgeon. A subsequent study is proposed to further investigate fixed focal points, their implications for remote diagnostics, and potential applications in other imaging modalities. The dataset, covering 10 years and containing over 700 sites, provides detailed information on daily operations, including observation procedures, equipment types, and site characteristics. About 1/3 of sites experience some type of malfunction, with the three most common issues being electronics problems (43%), physical damage (27%), and other issues (20%). It is discovered that electronics problems are more prevalent in rural areas (31%) than in urban areas (21%), whereas physical damage is more common in urban environments (34%) than in more remote locations (25%). The research finds that sites situated at high elevations (45%) or in close proximity to bodies of water (31%) are more prone to experiencing electronics issues. Conversely, weather van stations are more susceptible to physical damage (43%), particularly those deployed in urban settings (40%) or at airports (39%). The investigation also finds that sites relying on manual observations are more likely to encounter electronics problems (51%), especially those adopting the traditional manual methods of temperature and precipitation collection. On the other hand, sites employing automatic drivers' methods are more vulnerable to physical damage (41%), particularly those based in urban environments (40%). The research identifies potential ways to mitigate these issues, such as recognizing the effectiveness of urban-based sites in preventing physical damage and targeting resources at remote or special-interest stations to reduce electronics problems. Furthermore, the analysis suggests that national weather services could save resources by consolidating observations at remote or special-interest sites, thereby potentially alleviating financial burdens and addressing other challenges such as the growing costs of replacing and maintaining observation technology and the shortage of skilled technicians needed to troubleshoot and maintain existing systems. 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) research: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
To address this challenge, we introduced a comprehensive framework consisting of three phases.
Firstly, the Advanced Open Vocabulary Assisted OCR (AVAO) method was used to help the model learn how to recognize new characters.
Next, the Refined Mask Attention (RMA) module refined the mask attention to accurately capture the entire new word, even if it's composed of unseen characters.
Finally, the Word-based Attention for OOV (WAO) layer provided an attention layer that helped the word embedding lock information about seen words, thereby improving the recognition of OOV words.
To evaluate our approach, we used a combination of seen and OOV sentences from the Internet Shopping Evaluation (ISE) dataset.
The results demonstrated that our WAO framework had superior performance compared to the baseline models and outperformed the baseline in both seen and OOV scenarios.

While it's well-documented that this algorithm converges when a solution exists, a linear convergence rate is achieved only if both the solution and the reference coupling have the same support. Considering that structured stochastic processes can provide a more informed starting point for the reference coupling, selectively sampling from the reference coupling is not necessarily linearly convergent. This paper proposes a novel approach called the dynamic batching algorithm, which accelerates the Sinkhorn iteration by taking advantage of the structure in the data. By incorporating a sampling mechanism that utilizes probability weights to guide sampling, the algorithm yields superior results. We derive convergence evidence for this approach, specifically showing that dynamic batching is capable of achieving geometric convergence at a rate of O(1/n) when working with matrix manifolds, outperforming the standard Sinkhorn algorithm in both speed and accuracy. We also present the results of a computational experiment, demonstrating that the algorithm can obtain accurate solutions with minimal iterations, and in some cases, achieve solution accuracy in just a single iteration. We further provide an updated version of the algorithm, dynamic batching with stochastic averaging, which incorporates stochastic averaging, resulting in faster convergence and more robust solution acquisition, especially in cases where solution is either saturated or ill-defined. This is substantiated by the results of a computational study, showing the increased robustness of the averaging step. We also provide geometric convergence evidence for this updated approach, demonstrating a rate of O(1/n^2) with stochastic averaging. Two additional studies are presented, demonstrating that our algorithm is capable of producing reliable solutions for diverse datasets, and, in a computational experiment, showing that a hierarchical sampling strategy is necessary for achieving minimal coupling support when solution is identified. We present the results of a comprehensive ablation study, showing the importance of incorporating stochastic averaging for robust solution acquisition, and, in a computational study, revealing that our algorithm is capable of producing reliable solutions for a diverse range of probabilistic groundings, including uniform probabilistic groundings, Gaussian probabilistic groundings, and probabilistic groundings defined by continuous functions. We further propose a novel approach, progressive pruning, which involves progressively removing mass from the algorithm's state during the Sinkhorn iteration. This is made possible by leveraging structured stochastic processes to establish a prior probability distribution over the algorithm's state. Although progressive pruning has a higher computational overhead, we show that it is capable of delivering more accurate solutions with fewer iterations. We provide convergence evidence for this novel approach, showing that it yields a linear convergence rate. We also present the

A key limitation of these techniques is the tradeoff between scalability and validity: methods that handle a large number of qubits tend to produce negative probabilities, whereas those that guarantee a correct probability distribution cannot be scaled. To address these concerns, we propose a new scheme that combines both principles. Current mapping approaches utilize various metrics such as leverage, forward visibility, and occupancy to create detailed maps but tend to be model-based, which can prove challenging for mobile robots due to their inherent sensor limitations. Conversely, self-supervised learning offers an alternative for mapping, but existing deep learning-based approaches struggle to provide detailed maps as required by tasks like motion planning. Our proposed solution, the Map-N-Go algorithm, utilizes an efficient strategy to generate maps based on key features such as paths, obstacles, and surround views. It consists of two main components: (1) an online learning process that converts camera images into a set of discriminative viewpoints, and (2) a map augmentation process that incorporates new information to generate a detailed map. Our approach is evaluated using simulations in complex environments and found to outperform state-of-the-art methods including cartography and learning-based mapping. Furthermore, we have found that using Map-N-Go's learned view representation, we can achieve a significant reduction of at least 60% in 3D mapping latency and 75% in memory storage compared to traditional methods. Additionally, our method allows for seamless integration of tasks like motion planning by providing a detailed map, and our findings demonstrate the efficacy of our approach compared to existing model-based methods. Lastly, based on our understanding of the problem, we have developed a practical evaluation of the current state-of-the-art, showing that our proposed solution can offer a similar level of performance as that of Google cartographer by applying our learned view representation to construct a map. This paper presents a novel method for designing two-dimensional zero-complementary array code sequences using complex number roots of a polynomial function. Examples of these code sequences are given in the form of two-dimensional arrays consisting of complex numbers, and the code family is further expanded by utilizing different values of the variable in the given polynomial function. Two-dimensional arrays consisting of real numbers can be obtained by substituting specific values into the code sequences. Utilizing the developed code sequences, two-dimensional arrays are constructed that exhibit favorable two-dimensional correlation properties. These code sequences possess modulated complementary code orthogonal sequences properties, and the resulting two-dimensional arrays can be employed in the design of ultra-narrow band, high data rate, and low power consumption communication systems. Furthermore, the code sequences are shown to be used in the construction of efficient 2-D phased array antennas that are capable of efficiently transmitting and receiving multi-directional signals with minimal interference from adjacent data in the frequency domain. This occurs due to the unique correlation properties of the code sequences as a function of frequency, and the potential implementation of the code sequences is discussed using a VNA prototype setup. Experimental results from the prototype demonstrate that the proposed two-dimensional arrays can be effectively utilized in the development of efficient phased array antennas. These code sequences are applied to an antenna setup in the form of a Uniform Parabolic 2-D Array, and the efficiency of the code sequences is evaluated through the analysis of the resulting far-field radiation pattern. To achieve this objective, the code sequences are used to drive a phased array antenna that employs the developed code sequences as its corresponding voltage excitation levels. This results in the establishment of a unique radiation pattern where all the antenna elements collaborate to create a strong main lobe while maintaining low side lobes. The propagation of waves through the space between the antenna elements is taken into consideration in the code performance and is seen to have a negligible impact on the correlation properties of the code. To confirm this assumption, the code performance is evaluated by accounting for the size of the elements in the array and the distance between the elements. This occurs due to the modulation of the phase of the waves by the elements in the array, and the potential implementation of the code sequences in a phased array antenna has been successfully tested. Health Records (EHRs) has emerged as a crucial area of study, as machine learning models can assist healthcare professionals in decision-making to enhance overall healthcare quality. Advances in recent years have seen the development of sequential or graph-based models aiming to tackle this task. Despite the complexity and diversity of EHR data, which can be visualized as a multi-layered, interconnected network (heterogeneous graph), past studies have neglected these essential aspects. Moreover, existing methods that deal with graph diversity are not directly applicable to EHR data due to its unique properties such as the presence of dominant hub nodes. To address this limitation, we introduce the Heterogeneous Similarity Graph Neural Network (HSGNN), a novel, generic, and realistic framework for analyzing diverse EHR data. Our approach involves creating a diverse, representative patient graph from extracted features and annotations, and then trains a graph neural network with an end-to-end framework to predict patient outcomes. To reflect the complex, multi-faceted linkages between patient features, we incorporate different types of connections within the patient graph, such as similarity relationships and causal associations. In addition, we use node attribute embeddings to convey rich information about patients. To further improve robustness and prevent overfitting, we incorporate a robust categorical attention network. Our method's effectiveness is supported by the results of experiments, which consist of five real-world EHR datasets from various institutions. A thorough evaluation of our method reveals that it performs better and more robustly than existing, leading baselines, and our study confirms the relation between our method's predictions and actual real-world healthcare outcomes. As an innovative and knowledge-driven approach to analyzing diverse EHR data, we believe that our method has promising applications and can make a significant contribution to improving healthcare systems. Our method's source code will be publicly available and released under an open-source license. {url} https://github.com/kelski/HSGNN.git {url} doi: 10.1016/J.JMVA.2022.02.024. The HSGNN paper won the Best Paper Award at ESANN'2021 and was selected as an Outstanding Paper at KDD'2021. It also placed 2nd overall in the 2021 KDD Social KDD competition (4th place overall), where participants aimed to forecast patient health outcomes from EHR data. The HSGNN method earned an official Mention in 4th Place by the organizers (KDD'2021 Social Patient Outcomes), and a Supplemental Award was presented

From a free energy model, we calculate the electrostatic potential and number of water and ions within the boundary using coupled differential equations. We discover that solvent effects profoundly impact double-layer behavior, particularly in situations involving small particles. Additionally, we find that assuming solvent effects can be combined with size effects can accurately replicate precise molecular simulation results, yielding effective charges and densities that align with these simulations. This suggests a possible method to determine key characteristics of flexible materials and charged surfaces. Further analysis reveals that assuming solvability can lead to inaccuracies when considering specific surface charges and ion sizes, but that solvent effects consistently affect double-layer behavior. However, assuming solvability yields a computationally viable means to calculate effective surface charges and densities from experimental data, potentially unveiling hidden properties of flexible materials and charged surfaces. Nonetheless, we identify circumstances in which solvability assumptions may cause substantial discrepancies and neglecting solvent effects can lead to counterintuitive outcomes, even if effective charges and densities yield accurate results. Moreover, we find that solvent effects consistently impact double-layer behavior and neglecting solvent effects can cause double layers to become unstable if not counteracted by surface charges. Notably, we show that including size effects can stabilize such layers and resolve such instability, but fails to eliminate the required charges. Finally, we investigate how charging flexible materials can significantly alter the predicted densities of ions and solvent within the double layer, with potential implications for understanding material synthesis and chemical reactions. From a fundamental perspective, we see that assuming solvability can uncover the roles of free charges within the double layer, predicting that flexible materials may hold an excess of charges, while also identifying further research needs to investigate the properties of fabricated materials and their potential to behave as predicted.

To improve point cloud registration for dynamic scenes, deep learning-based approaches have shown potential.  Despite their accuracy, deep learning-based solutions often provide little insight, which is a safety concern.  To bridge this gap, our paper introduces an approach that involves selectively removing points with inconsistent motion patterns from point clouds.  By using normal vectors to represent motion features, we can achieve point cloud registration using a single rotation transformation across consecutive scans.  To enhance the stability of our method, we can combine multiple registrations with different constraint levels.  Experimental results indicate that with strict consistency checks, our method can achieve an average registration error of 3.25 cm, which compares favorably to the state-of-the-art.  Additionally, by relaxing the constraint on maximum point number, we can achieve even smaller average registration errors of 1.83 cm.  Notably, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods while requiring only a constant number of operations regardless of the point number.  Moreover, the proposed technique of identifying co-planar points allows us to develop other algorithms for reducing point cloud registration errors.  By building upon this technique, for example, we can produce accurate per-point corrections with the ability to ablate the corresponding results from 4.23 cm to 3.55 cm in terms of average registration error.  Our technique of identifying co-planar points can also be used in computing NDT octree correlations.  It significantly improves the accuracy of point cloud registration from 6.74 cm to 4.55 cm and even to 3.55 cm when applying the constraint on maximum point number.  These improvements in accuracy prove that identifying co-planar points is beneficial for both direct per-point correction and point cloud registration.  Furthermore, the technique of using normals to represent motion features in point clouds can be applied in providing a visual representation of the outcome of point cloud registration. Lastly, the process of selectively removing points with inconsistent motion features can be utilized in implementing per-point correction with robustness against outliers by performing the operation only on the points that are consistent. This experiment investigates the evolution of electronic temperature in polycrystalline Nb metal, a material exhibiting correlation effects due to its strong interaction, after being exposed to high-fluence X-ray pulses. Two distinct methods were employed to evaluate the electron's temperature: first, by analyzing X-ray absorption near edge structure and Core-Hole Yield following X-ray pulses, and second, by examining X-ray Transient Linear Polarization. To compute the electronic temperature, density functional theory was relied upon for initial calculations and the DYSERteria computer code was used for model-independent analyses based on experimental reflectivity data. Results show that the electronic temperature peaks at 5-6 eV, significantly exceeding the phonon maximum temperature due to interplay between photon absorption and electron-lattice interactions. Moreover, reflections and small-angle diffraction experiments indicate that the electronic temperature reaches its peak earlier than that of phonons, with a relation that can be attributed to the specific X-ray absorption mechanism involving multiple processes. This relationship is understood as stemming from a conditional phase shift induced by nuclear rearrangement triggered by photon absorption from the X-ray pulse. With an exponentially decreasing electronic temperature tail that persists until at least 200 ps after excitation, observations suggest the occurrence of multiple phonon cascades, facilitated by the sustained X-ray absorption and absorption-induced nuclear correlations. Furthermore, observation of phonon cascades allows for direct assessment of the phonon population decay rate. The experimental findings are supported by an analytical model accounting for electronic excitation, nuclear rearrangement, and photon emission, with results indicating that nuclear correlations remain intact or strengthened upon X-ray excitation. The experimental and theoretical investigation reveals the interconnected nature of electronic and nuclear dynamics across an immense range of timescales, driven by a quantum flash that triggers nuclear dynamics. Ultimately, the study shows that electronic temperature can serve as a reliable indicator of nuclear temperature due to the close correlation between their respective distributions. As a result, the electronic temperature can be used as a more accessible measure for monitoring nuclear dynamics. The observed nuclear dynamics persisting until at least 200 ps hold significant implications for materials science, chemistry, and physics, where ionization-driven nuclear rearrangement may offer new, controllable pathways for achieving novel crystal structures with potential applications in the development of metastable and enthalpy-driven phase transitions. Modulation Classification (AMC) exhibits enhanced performance compared to traditional methods even in harsh wireless environments, but this can be compromised by targeted adversarial attacks that inject noise into wireless channels. This paper presents a new method to counter such attacks by using a Deep Neural Network to accurately identify the attack origin before feeding data into a classifier. The proposed approach incorporates information about signal phase, power, and time from the received signal to determine the attacker's angle of incidence. Simulations indicate that this method is effective across different signal SNRs and numbers of attackers. Although limited by its reliance on 2-D search with some approximation, this method provides a reliable safeguard against such attacks. Our results show successful identification of up to 7 attackers per room using this method. Moreover, the proposed approach has the advantage of being largely hardware-independent, reducing the need for extensive experiments on costly hardware. Although the described setup is small and the proposed method has its own restrictions, this technique has the potential to be scalable to more complex scenarios. ary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by the Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis explores the mechanics of a cosmic collider through two types of primordial features. Firstly, we consider oscillating primordial features, encompassing cases of massive field oscillations and oscillatory features in the inflationary potential. Secondly, we look at any sharp feature within an inflationary model. These features can induce unsuppressed quantum fluctuations in heavy fields, leaving detectable signatures in primordial non-Gaussian patterns, and revealing details about the spectra of these heavy degrees of freedom. Notably, these signatures might be within the threshold of detection in upcoming surveys of cosmic structures. Moreover, we observe how the analytical approach to the cosmic collider signals becomes exact in specific limit conditions. These concern an approximately de Sitter background, a sharp momentum cutoff (at least one order of magnitude greater than the curvature scale), and a tree-level process involving two external particles and one propagating particle. This latter property makes the cosmological collider more analogous to an ultra-violet complete particle collider. Finally, it is also worth noting that slow-roll conditions do not necessarily guarantee that the features are within the scope of the cosmic collider, and other parameters such as the slope of the potential and the mass of the oscillating field can make the features more or less pronounced or even invert their signs. Furthermore, there may be an approximation error of about ten percent, and a more detailed calculation shows that the signals can become suppressed by a factor of about 100 due to a broader momentum range of the intermediate field. To address this issue, a framework called LaViSE is proposed, allowing regularized self-supervised models to provide more accurate and informative visual representations. LaViSE is comprised of two main components: 1) a visual encoder for deriving dense image features, and 2) a contrastive predictor that fine-tunes these features to capture more semantic details. The framework is evaluated on multiple datasets, and the results show that LaViSE can improve model interpretability while maintaining their accuracy. Additionally, a method is proposed for generating meaningful images using the LaViSE predictor. Compared to previous techniques, LaViSE produces higher quality results, and the code is available at https://github.com/agentadm/lavise. It is also demonstrated that LaViSE can enhance classification models by leveraging its explanatory power. Furthermore, a comparison between self-supervised and contrastive prediction approaches indicates that contrastive models are more susceptible to overfitting and therefore, simpler regularization methods, such as random erasing, can be effective in improving the robustness and interpretability of self-supervised models. Finally, an investigation into the effect of random erasing on different levels of visual representations reveals that applying it on high-level features is more beneficial, and the greatest improvement is observed when combining it with other techniques, such as cutout, to augment the training dataset. The study shows that applying random erasing on high-level features of pre-trained models can significantly improve their generalization and in-distribution performance, even when the models are previously well-trained. The presented research is the first to show such a combination of hand-designed and data augmentation methods, and the potential of applying these techniques to other areas of vision research is a promising direction for further investigation. These findings are a solid foundation for advancing the field of visual explanation and are supported by extensive qualitative and quantitative analysis and experiments. Moreover, the proposed methods are transferable to other tasks, such as few-shot learning, as demonstrated by an experiment showing that a LaViSE model pre-trained on ImageNet can seamlessly switch to object categorization with only five shots per category without any further fine-tuning. The results indicate that the visual representations learned by LaViSE are highly flexible and can be used for other tasks with minimal adjustment. In summary, the research focused on developing techniques to explain self-supervised models by incorporating principles of contrastive learning and regularizing the models using data augmentation methods. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. A compelling example of this relationship is the behavior of a Bose gas confined to a one-dimensional space, where the presence of an infinite number of conservation laws prevents the system from reaching thermal equilibrium and constraining the system's dynamics. Through an experimental approach and by examining one-dimensional characteristics, researchers discovered that the process of thermalization can be utilized to determine the system's spatial dimension. Notably, when the system is subjected to a quench, and we analyze the spatial correlations of the system at a later time while adjusting the interaction strength, we find that the system behaves like a system in zero dimensions. Remarkably, we can accurately describe this unique thermalization process using a microscopic theory that is applicable to diverse systems of different dimensions, and by comparing these predictions with the experimental findings, we can precisely determine the system's spatial dimension. This approach opens a fresh pathway for exploring quantum phenomena that emerge from the interplay of many-body interactions and the spatial dimension of a system, and our method enables us to distinguish these unique states experimentally. 
The research is available at Phys. Rev. X 11, 041032 (2021), and Y B Wang et al, Science Advances, 6, eabc3342, 2020. By subjecting the system to a quench, and by examining the various spatial correlations at different times, we found that the system behaves like a zero-dimensional system, and these observations align with the predictions of the theoretical model.  Lastly, we discuss the possibility of employing our experimental approach to investigate other quantum states that emerge in diverse many-body systems by analyzing the spatial correlations, and our method has the potential to contribute to the field of quantum simulation.

Although straightforward, incorporating wavelet transformations into machine learning pipelines leads to a crucial challenge: the lack of a gradient operator. This study establishes a gradient operator for two-dimensional Haar wavelet transformations. Additionally, the study incorporates Haar wavelet transforms into activation layers to observe an increase in the test accuracy of the MNIST dataset, reaching approximately 97.04%. The largest application involves using Haar wavelet transforms to analyze the Cosmic Microwave Background data, employing a gradient-based optimization procedure to locate signal patches that contain diffuse foreground signals, thereby facilitating data compression. This study investigates the issue of inferring constraints from observational data of an agent's compliant behavior. Experimental validation is performed to verify that the proposed method successfully identifies the most relevant constraints an agent is expected to follow. Furthermore, these constraints can be generalized and applied to novel agents with different structures and reward schemes. In contrast to existing methods that are primarily designed for tabular settings, specific types of constraints, or assume environment dynamics, the presented framework can autonomously learn any type of Markovian constraint within complex high-dimensional environments without the need for model-based representations. Evaluations across diverse scenarios in synthetic and real-world robotic settings demonstrate the efficacy of the framework. An additional analysis reveals that the framework provides explicit bounds on its uncertainty regarding the constraints an agent is expected to follow. This characteristic can be exploited for improving privacy considerations by releasing upper bounds on the number of relevant constraints an agent is expected to follow. Such release of statistics holds significant potential for the protection of user data in applications like RL policy tuning and social learning. Finally, the presentation outlines possible future research directions that can provide more transparent, explainable, and robust decision-making processes for RL applications. This includes the development of formal notions of environment-induced errors, the exploration of methods for detecting time-varying constraints, and the creation of an empirical model to analyze the robustness of the framework. A successful application of the framework has been demonstrated in a real-world robotic setup, the XACRO robot. This robot navigates through obstacle-filled environments and picks up objects within the AirSim simulator. Due to the constraints an agent is expected to follow during physical interactions, the robot can safely operate in both simulated and real-world settings. They comprise the central component of the robot's software architecture and serve as the core framework for robust and compliant decision-making processes within the XACRO project. Most network measures were initially developed for simple networks and later extended to weighted networks.
Initially, weighted networks were studied by converting weights into distances and analyzing them with new measures, ignoring the original edge weights' information or modifying it completely.
We suggest that for weighted network construction, an intermediate approach is taken, where distances based on edge weights are considered, and an efficient measure of network centrality is proposed for weighted networks, which incorporates the edge-weight information.
This measure, called the Rooted PageRank (RP) and is defined by iterating from a given starting node with specified edge weights and directions, and it includes options for dynamic starting nodes and edge weight definitions. 
We demonstrate that for weighted network construction, an efficient version of RP is presented, and its convergence is analyzed with a theoretical explanation for the speeding-up technique.
This technique is then tested on six different data sets for the calculation of the centrality of weighted networks, and the results show that for the calculation of the centrality of weighted networks, an averaged RP is more natural than a starting node-dependent version. 
Moreover, this measure is simple to calculate and generalizes previous centrality measures, and the technique with which it is calculated is efficient for large networks, and the results demonstrate its value in identifying key components within the networks, and the visual analysis shows that for the calculation of the centrality of weighted networks, an interpreted and analyzed version of RP is more natural than a technical version.

A vertex cover of a hypergraph is a subset of vertices that incorporates all the edges and edges spanning k vertices in the hypergraph. Here, a vertex cover is referred to as minimal if none of its proper subsets serve as vertex covers. The paper's main objective is to investigate upper limits of the minimal edge cover and vertex cover numbers for hypergraphs possessing the property C(k, ρ). Specifically, it studies hypergraphs with the property C(3, 2), and it demonstrates that not much is yet understood about general hypergraphs possessing the property C(3, 2). Furthermore, it introduces the concept of a hypergraph's l-color abstract covering, and it studies the relationship between the size of its color classes and the total number of colors required. A dual concept to vertex cover number is also introduced - the dual number - which represents the minimum size of a subset of edges that covers all the vertices in the hypergraph. Properties of hypergraphs possessing the property C(3, 2) in relation to their dual numbers and vertex cover numbers are investigated. Specifically, it is shown that there are hypergraphs with the property C(3, 2) whose dual numbers tend towards n^2/2 and whose minimum size vertex cover numbers are also near n^2/2. It is observed that for hypergraphs allowing a covering of size n/2 with edges of order 3, a bound of n^2/2 is also a limit for their dual numbers. Moreover, it is shown that there are hypergraphs with the property C(3, 2) whose total number of edges is near n^3/6, and various upper bounds for their total number of edges are investigated. It is explored whether there are hypergraphs with the property C(3, 2) whose total number of edges is near n^3/6 plus a linear factor. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when dealing with large, complex ontologies, enabling easier comprehension and exploration. However, existing visualisation tools predominantly focus on hierarchical structures and overlook other types of associations. This paper introduces OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation system designed to seamlessly balance the exploration of all concept relationships and large hierarchical structures. OntoPlot's novel hybrid visualisation incorporates icicle plots, interactive elements, and space-efficient visual compression to enhance understanding and reduce visual clutter. Through a user study involving domain experts, we compared OntoPlot's usability to that of Protégé, the industry-standard ontology editor, finding that OntoPlot surpassed expectations in facilitating association-related tasks and earned widespread endorsement from domain specialists. It provides visualisations for millions of concepts, enabling users to explore the Open Biological Standards Ontology, the Gene Ontology, and the SNOMED-CT. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's success in explaining various cognitive aspects, its practical application is constrained by the computationally intensive task of repeatedly updating this mental model in real-time. This research investigates whether simpler, less demanding models can effectively predict human behavior, and whether such models can be used to create more efficient artificial agents that mimic human performance without the need for complex mental updates. By employing a novel method of identifying patterns in mental models, we discovered that a simplified strategy that relies solely on short-term memory is surprisingly effective in predicting both human behavior and its time delays, as it leverages expectations of recent sensory patterns to forecast upcoming events. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our simplified approach is more resilient to variations in human subjects, when compared to more elaborate models, and that it offers better performance than a standard policy network design. Moreover, we observed a striking similarity between our model's internal states, including a temporary 'perceptual perisaccadic delay', and the temporary disruption of processing during saccadic eye movements. This finding suggests that our internal state may reflect transitions between task-related states, and that the temporary disruption of processing during saccades creates opportunities for 'gaps' in mental updates. Interestingly, we found that our simplified approach outperforms the standard active inference model, likely due to internal noise, perceptual delays, and computational limitations, and that our internal state is reminiscent of processing transitions similar to those observed during eye movements. This research is a step towards developing simplified models that can efficiently replicate human behavior, both in terms of the tasks themselves and the temporal delays involved, and that our models are consistent with cognitive transitions, including the temporary disruption of processing during attention and perception. By employing these simplified models, we created efficient perceiver-peractor policies that mimic human performance without requiring detailed mental updates, and showed that our approach is superior to current state-of-the-art policies. By developing simpler models, we now have more control over the dynamics of active inference, and our approach is robust against variations in human subjects, and is more compact than current state-of-the-art policies. Based on these findings, we are confident that our approach can lead to the creation of more efficient artificial agents that mimic human performance without requiring detailed mental updates, and that our approach will contribute to understanding the interface between perception and action in cognitive systems. We developed the Binding Energy Evaluation Platform (BEEP) to create a comprehensive database containing the full range of binding energies between molecules and an amorphous water surface model. BEEP employs highly automated quantum chemical methods to identify multiple binding sites on water clusters, allowing for the precise calculation of binding energies. Our research involved computing binding energy distributions for 21 molecules and 87 different water cluster subtypes, encompassing 279 distinct binding sites. We analyzed these findings along with 11 additional systems from previous studies to understand how polar non-covalent and hydrogen-bonded binding sites contribute to the overall binding energy landscape. We analyzed the correlation between molecular properties and hydrogen-bonding patterns, revealed significant disparities between experimentally and computationally determined binding energies, and established statistical relationships between these binding energies and molecular properties. By creating an empirically-driven distribution of binding energies, we provide a framework that can be generalized to predict complex binding scenarios involving larger molecules and multi-component ices. BEEP is designed as an end-to-end automated code suite capable of being reconfigured to study a wide range of ice-grain surface binding sites, making it an accessible tool for researchers to explore and expand the understanding of binding energies involving various molecules and water clusters, and of both traditional and complex ices. The BEEP code is available at https://github.com/RGonzalezAguilera/BEEP, and our full database is available online at https://doi.org/10.35092/uni-heide-ak.2029888. As the interest in meta-learning grows, there is a pressing need to establish its theoretical foundations, especially in terms of learning adaptable representations. In this research, we tackle the problem of multi-task linear regression where multiple related tasks share a common, low-dimensional linear representation. Our study provides effective, sample-efficient methods to address the dual challenges of learning a shared feature set from related tasks and transferring this knowledge to unseen tasks. This work sheds light on the central issue of meta-learning. Furthermore, we present theoretical limits on the minimum sample size required to learn these shared features. Our findings indicate that a specific, linearly-related set of tasks can achieve optimal adaptation when represented linearly. This study helps lay the groundwork for future research in this area. We verify the practical validity of our theoretical findings through testing on simulated data. This research also contributes to a better comprehension of meta-learning in its own right by extracting a fundamental learning problem from it. Although it's a small step, it may help to illuminate the still somewhat enigmatic field of meta-learning. The related problem is extremely similar to several well-known challenges like PCA and it's hopeful that the methods developed here could be applied to those problems as well. The constructed synthetic data also allows for a thorough assessment of the theoretical approximations and reveals that representation learning can be very efficient in unseen tasks but that there are some cases where double sampling is more efficient than single sampling. -art machine translation models can aid in adapting to low-resource languages despite limited data, albeit resulting in oversized models that are impractical for deployment. To combat this, Knowledge Distillation is an often-used technique to create high-performance yet lightweight models. This paper initially assesses its application in compressing MT models, particularly for languages with scarce training data, examining eight languages in the process. Notably, it is discovered that distillation-based model performance variability heavily relies on several preconditions, making it a somewhat unreliable compression approach. To improve on this, we explore post-training quantization as a means to compress these models. Ultimately, while distillation was found effective in certain domains, it was determined that quantization produces more consistent results and is a more reliable compression method. Additional analysis reveals that both methods have differing implications for in-domain and out-of-domain translation, with quantization offering a bonus in the latter, specifically when it comes to preserving translation accuracy during 12 months of live deployment on mTurk. Specifically, it is found that preserving 12 months of translation quality using quantized models is 90%, effectively making these models practical for deployment in settings where resources are constrained. Finally, to enhance both models, it is demonstrated that combining them results in variable improvements of translation quality within the models, depending on the domain and language in question. Moreover, it is observed that leveraging both models leads to consistent gains in the domain-adaptation scenario, specifically when models are adapted for domain translation tasks. This, in turn, is shown to result in quality increases ranging from 1.0 to 2.0 BLEU points in different domain translation scenarios. To facilitate future research, we have made our datasets, code, and models available at https://github.commiunity.net/MULTINL_GMT/. We welcome researchers interested in deploying these models in real-world settings to join our GitHub community and gain access to related resources. The Turan density of F, denoted by pi(F), is defined as the limit of the maximum number of edges over the total possible number of edges as the number of vertices approaches infinity. Erdos-Stone-Simonovits' theorem established that the set of possible Turan densities for 2-uniform graphs is infinite, and for 3-uniform graphs, irrational Turan densities have been discovered, disproving a previous conjecture. We investigate whether irrational Turan densities exist in certain cases and show that the Lagrangian density of a specific 3-uniform graph is sqrt(3)/3, resulting in an irrational Turan density, which answers an open question posed by Baber and Talbot. We then define an equivalence relation over the set of possible vertex sets in 3-uniform graphs and demonstrate its impact on the structure of their joint distribution. We show that for any pair of 3-uniform graphs F and G that have equal densities to the square root of 3/3 in this setting, the maximum number of edges in F-free 3-uniform graphs on n vertices is less than or equal to the maximum number of edges in G-free 3-uniform graphs on n vertices. We utilize linear programming to identify the maximum number of edges in both F-free and G-free 3-uniform graphs on 121 vertices. We conclude that the set of possible Turan densities for 3-uniform graphs is infinite, and for a specific case where one graph has an equality with 3/3 and the other with 2/sqrt(2), we demonstrate that the maximum number of edges in both F-free and G-free 3-uniform graphs on n vertices approaches infinity as n approaches infinity. We also show that for a specific case where one graph has an equality with 3/3 and the other is omitted, the maximum number of edges in F-free 3-uniform graphs on n vertices exceeds the maximum number of edges in G-free 3-uniform graphs on n vertices, which approaches infinity as n approaches infinity. We then investigate whether irrational Turan densities exist in this specific case and show that for any pair of 3-uniform graphs F and H, the maximum number of edges in F-free 3-uniform graphs on n vertices exceeds the maximum number of edges in H-free 3-uniform graphs on n vertices,

the Variational Separability Verifier (VSV), to identify the closest separable state of an arbitrary quantum state with minimal deviation in norm. This algorithm employs a variational principle, leveraging the fact that the closest separable state lies within the convex hull of orthogonal projection operators corresponding to entangled subspaces. It then uses an orthogonally compliant unitary (OCU) ansatz to approximate these projection operators. By iterating circuit applications and adaptations, along with measurements of key quantum states, the algorithm iteratively refines its approximation of the closest separable state. Notably, circuit adaptations are guided by comparing the computed quantum state with the estimated closest separable state in each iteration. Our experimental results demonstrate that the VSV algorithm successfully identifies the closest separable state for certain entangled states within a reasonable number of iterations. Furthermore, we prove that the true separability distance from an arbitrary quantum state can be approximated to a certain precision, and our findings validate this theoretical result through experimental evidence. The algorithm's performance is also evaluated on randomly generated quantum states with varying dimensions, and the effects of noise on its operations are assessed. Moreover, we extend the algorithm to determine the closest k-separable state as a generalized form, where k-separable states include both separable and k-extendable states. We assert that the VSV algorithm serves as a robust tool for detecting entanglement and could contribute to ongoing research on the geometrically convex structure of separable states. Our work is expected to facilitate the assessment of entanglement benchmarks, providing a novel method for characterizing non-separable quantum systems. The algorithm could also be adapted for detection and characterization of multi-partite entangled states, and might provide an alternative to traditional entanglement monotones. We anticipate that the implementation of the VSV algorithm in noisy conditions will provide practical insights for real-world applications. The algorithm can be seamlessly applied to multi-partite systems, and the computational efficiency of the OCU ansatz makes it a suitable candidate for NISQ devices. The theoretical and experimental findings presented here are anticipated to inspire further research on the structural properties of separable states, as well as the development of novel entanglement characterization methods. The source code for the VSV algorithm will be made available upon request. The NISQ circuit code is accessible via the Q# platform on Microsoft Quantum, and the Arquana Quantum Cloud, where the results described in this work were obtained. Finally, the work presented here is conforming to all ethical standards in research.

Prior research in a slab geometry setting showed that the drive mechanism requires collisions, but our simulations show that this is not the case in slab or tokamak environments. Our simulations show that the instability can occur in the electron temperature gradient without collisions and that the largest driving forces come from Landau interactions. Additionally, our simulations show that the energy from these interactions is stored in electron distribution functions, particularly at the resonance frequency. We found that the stability of such distributions is highly probable and that the only way to sustain the magnetic islands is if there is a balance between the drive and damping mechanisms. We have identified several mechanisms that can adequately damp the electron distribution, including collisions, electrostatic turbulence, anisotropic electron temperature damping, and MHD magnetic reconnections. We believe that microtearing modes have the potential to be a promising means of achieving the necessary magnetic reconnections for energy breakdown in future fusion devices. Our findings also provide an explanation for the observed scaling of power loss with electron temperature in the edge plasma of tokamaks. Finally, our research is further reflected in an analytical model that captures the essential aspects of microtearing mode physics. Our results are further confirmed through comparisons of the simulation and the analytical models. We have used the McFlux extended MHD code to simulate the stellarator NSTX-S1 device and our results show that the simulation agrees well with the experimental data, specifically in terms of both the location and size of the edge magnetic island. Our simulation shows that the island is caused by the balance between the microtearing mode and other mechanisms in the edge plasma. Our results demonstrate that the balance is purely based on the electron temperature. We have used the McFlux code to simulate a stellarator device and our results show that the microtearing mode is capable of generating edge turbulence. Our results show that the mode is caused by a combination of the electron temperature gradient and the magnetic geometry. Our simulation shows that the size of the island is directly proportional to the Maxwellian damping rate and the machine parameters. The increasing use of high-bandwidth applications such as online gaming, virtual reality, and high-definition video streaming require networks to have robust bandwidth supplies. One effective strategy for enhancing WiFi network performance is to implement channel bonding, which can increase available bandwidth by merging multiple channels into a single, wider channel. However, to protect against performance degradation caused by interference, it is often necessary to assign separate channels to different devices. These limitations can make implementing channel bonding on home networks difficult, as they typically consist of multiple access points and devices that compete for the same wireless medium. To overcome these challenges, we have developed a comprehensive system for leveraging channel bonding in home WiFi networks. Our solution, referred to as ChBoH, consists of a set of algorithms that work in unison to enable a shared, high-bandwidth channel for each device while minimizing the risk of performance degradation caused by interference. ChBoH begins by identifying and maximizing available resources for each device using a channel bonding detection algorithm, which identifies high-bandwidth applications and guarantees low-interference performance. Next, the assignment algorithm determines the optimal configuration for each device by prioritizing unidirectional channels to prevent performance degradation. These selections are then utilized by the scheduling algorithm to distribute maximum bandwidth to each device while minimizing exposure to interference in real-time. To evaluate the effectiveness of ChBoH, we conducted two experiments: one focused on performance optimization, and another centered on robustness.
